name: Chain of Responsibility
intent: Pass a request along a chain of handlers until one of them deals with it.
scenario: Expense requests need approval. A manager approves up to $1,000, a director up to $10,000, and the CEO anything above. The request goes to the first one who can approve it.
problem: Which approver handles a request depends on the amount. A single function with if/else for every level knows all approvers and their limits. Adding a level, or skipping one on holiday, means editing that function.
solution: Give each approver the same interface and a reference to the next approver. Each one either handles the request or passes it on. The client sends the request to the first link and does not need to know who ends up handling it.
pain: One function knows every approver and every limit
Adding a level means editing that function
Skipping an approver is impossible without changing code
benefits: Each approver knows only its own limit and the next link
A new level is a new handler inserted in the chain
Chains can be built or reordered at runtime
The client sends to the first handler and is done
whenToUse: More than one object may handle a request and the handler is not known in advance
You want to decouple the sender from the receivers
Middleware pipelines, event bubbling, validation steps, approval workflows
whenNotToUse: There is exactly one known handler: call it directly
Every step must run (that is a pipeline, not a chain where the first match wins)
Guaranteed handling is essential and a silent fall-off the end would be dangerous
pitfalls: A request may reach the end of the chain unhandled
Long chains are hard to debug: who handled it?
Accidental cycles in the chain loop forever
Order matters and is easy to get subtly wrong

roles.label: Handler
roles.description: Interface/base class: handle a request or pass it to the next.

roles.label: Concrete Handler
roles.description: One link in the chain with its own rule.

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Sends the request to the first handler.

quiz.question: An expense chain is manager (up to $1,000), director (up to $10,000), CEO (anything). Each link approves if it can, otherwise passes the request on. A $5,000 request is sent to the manager. What happens?
options: The manager approves it, because the first link in a chain always takes the request
The manager and director both review it, and the CEO signs off last
The request is rejected, because the manager's limit was exceeded and nobody else is asked
The manager forwards it, the director approves it, and the CEO never sees it
quiz.explanation: Each handler either handles the request or forwards it, and the first handler that can approve stops the chain. The manager cannot approve $5,000, so it forwards; the director can, so the CEO is never involved.

quiz.question: Someone builds the expense chain as manager then director and forgets to add the CEO. A $50,000 request is sent in, and nothing is approved, rejected or logged. What is the right fix?
options: Add a timeout on the client and retry the whole request again after a minute has passed
Let the director approve any amount, since the CEO link is missing and requests must not stall
Make the last link point back to the manager, so the request is retried through the chain
Add a final handler that rejects or escalates any request nobody handled, and records it
quiz.explanation: A request can fall off the end of a chain silently, so the chain should end with an explicit handler that fails loudly or escalates. Raising the director's limit changes the business rules, and retries or loops repeat the same dead end.

quiz.question: A web chain is Logging, Auth, RateLimit. The Logging handler logs the request and returns, treating it as handled, so Auth never runs. The requirement is that every request is logged, including rejected ones. What is the best fix?
options: Move Logging to the end of the chain, so it no longer blocks the links that follow it
Make Logging log and then call the next link
Merge Logging and Auth into a single handler, so both of them run on every request
Make Logging call Auth directly instead of through the chain, then return its result
quiz.explanation: Some steps must run for every request, so they do their work and pass the request on; only a rejecting step stops it. At the end of the chain, Logging would never see requests that Auth or RateLimit reject. Merging steps removes the flexibility of a chain.
